First, what do we mean by machine learning, and when would it be useful? Then, how do we turn a problem into inputs and an outcome to predict? We'll build a baseline, which gives us a simple reference point, and then a decision tree that asks questions about the inputs. You'll learn to fit the models in Python, follow a tree's predictions, and measure how many predictions are correct. Today we'll evaluate on the examples used for training. Whether the model works well on new examples is the central question for Lecture 2. ::: # AI, ML, and DL ::: {.notes} Let's start with three terms you've probably heard: artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning. They are related, but they don't mean exactly the same thing. We'll use a few familiar examples to separate them. ::: ## Where do AI, ML, and DL fit? {.slide-your-turn} Quick discussion: which of these might use AI, machine learning, or deep learning? - A spam detector 📧 - A basic calculator ➕ - A chatbot planning your holiday 💬 ::: {.notes} Take a look at these three systems: a spam detector, a basic calculator, and a chatbot helping plan a holiday. Which might use AI, machine learning, or deep learning? More importantly, what makes you think so? [Allow 30–60 seconds and take a few responses.] A spam detector could use rules written by a programmer, or it could learn from labeled emails. A basic calculator performs arithmetic using specified operations. A modern chatbot may use a deep learning language model, and it may also call tools such as search or a calculator. The name of the task doesn't tell us exactly how the system works. We need to know how it was built. ::: ## What are AI, ML, and DL? ![](img/ai-ml-dl.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" height="400px"} Our focus: learning from examples and applying what we learn to new cases. ::: {.notes} Read this diagram from the outside inward. Artificial intelligence is the broad field concerned with capabilities such as perception, reasoning, and planning. Machine learning is one approach within AI: learning patterns from data or experience. Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. These networks can learn representations that help them make predictions. Not every AI system learns from examples. Some use explicit rules or search. In this course, our focus is learning from examples and applying what we've learned to new cases. Let's make that concrete. ::: ## Image classification {.smaller} Searching photos for animals involves **image classification**. Imagine telling cats and foxes apart. How might we do this with traditional programming? With ML? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="35%"} ![](img/cat-or-fox.png) ::: ::: {.column width="65%"} | Image ID | Whiskers Present | Face Shape | Fur Colour | Label | |----------|------------------|------------|------------|-------| | 1 | Yes | Round | Mixed | Cat | | 2 | Yes | Round | Brown | Cat | | 3 | Yes | Pointed | Red | Fox | | 4 | Yes | Pointed | Red | Fox | | 5 | Yes | Round | Grey | Cat | ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Suppose we want to distinguish cats from foxes. What clues would you look for? [Take a few suggestions, then point to the table.] Here we've written down some possible clues. Each row describes one image. Whiskers, face shape, and fur colour are features: descriptions we could give a model. The label tells us the known answer, Cat or Fox. Image ID identifies the example; it isn't an animal characteristic. Which feature separates the labels in this tiny table? Face shape does, and fur colour also distinguishes these examples. Whiskers don't help here because every example has them. This is an illustrative table, not a reliable rule about all cats and foxes. The next question is who decides how to combine these clues. ::: ## Who writes the rules? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} **Traditional programming** We write the rules. **Pointed face + red fur** $\to$ Predict **fox** ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} **Machine learning** We provide labeled examples. **Features + cat/fox labels** $\to$ Learn a **prediction rule** ::: :::: ::: {.fragment} **What would happen with either approach if we encountered a fox with white fur?** ::: ::: {.notes} With traditional programming, we write the rule ourselves. For example, we might say: if the face is pointed and the fur is red, predict fox. With supervised machine learning, we provide examples of features and known labels. A learning algorithm uses those examples to fit a prediction rule. The resulting model may still contain rules; the difference is how we obtained them. What could go wrong with our hand-written rule? [Take a response, then reveal the white-fox question.] A white fox wouldn't satisfy the red-fur condition. A learned model could fail too if it relied on colour. It might succeed if it relied on face shape. We'd have to inspect or test it to know. Both approaches need evaluation on new cases. ::: ## DL approach: example :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](img/cat-or-fox.png) ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} - A neural network automatically learns which features to look at (edges $\rightarrow$ textures $\rightarrow$ objects). - No need to even specify face shape or fur colour. It learns relevant features on its own. ::: :::: ::: {.notes} In the table, we supplied features such as face shape and fur colour ourselves. An image neural network can instead start with pixel values and learn useful intermediate representations during training. Edges, textures, and objects give us an intuition for how representations can become more complex. That isn't a guaranteed sequence in every network, but it helps explain what we mean by learning features. For supervised cat-versus-fox classification, we still need labeled training images. We also need suitable data and evaluation. In this course, we'll focus on supervised learning with tables rather than training image networks. ::: ## Ways of learning from data {.smaller visibility="hidden"} - **Supervised learning:** predict targets from labeled examples - **Unsupervised learning:** discover structure without supplied targets - **Reinforcement learning:** learn actions through interaction and rewards - **Generative AI:** generate content; models can use several learning approaches - **Recommendation systems:** learn preferences, often combining multiple approaches These categories are not mutually exclusive. ::: {.notes} [Optional hidden slide; use only if a broader orientation is helpful.] Supervised learning uses examples with known targets. Unsupervised learning looks for structure without a supplied target for each example. Reinforcement learning learns actions through interaction and rewards. Generative AI describes systems that generate content, and recommendation systems describe an application. They can involve several learning approaches, so these aren't five mutually exclusive categories. Our course will focus on supervised learning: using known outcomes to learn how to predict unknown ones. ::: ## Supervised learning: inputs, targets, and predictions {.smaller} - **Inputs ($X$):** observations described by features, such as fur colour and face shape. - **Targets ($y$):** labels or values we want to predict, such as cat or fox. - **Training:** learn a model $f$ relating inputs to targets. - **Prediction:** use the model to predict targets for unseen examples. ![](img/sup-learning.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" height="280px"} ::: {.notes} Let's name the pieces of supervised learning. Capital X contains the inputs, described by features. Lowercase y contains the targets we want to predict. In our animal example, X contains descriptions of the images, and y contains Cat or Fox. During training, the algorithm uses X and y to learn a model, which we'll call f. During prediction, we give that fitted model the features of a new example, and it returns a predicted target. We don't give it the new example's answer. What would we need later to check whether the prediction was correct? [Pause for a response.] We'd need the actual label. Before we start fitting models, though, let's ask when ML is an appropriate tool. ::: # When should we use ML? ::: {.notes} Knowing how to fit a model is only part of the job. We also need to decide whether learning from data is a useful starting point for the problem. Let's compare situations where explicit rules, machine learning, or human judgment might make sense. ::: ## ❓❓ Rules, ML, or human judgment? {.slide-your-turn} Choose a starting point for each problem and explain why. Combinations are possible. - **(A)** Checking whether an email address ends with `@student.ubc.ca` - **(B)** Predicting which songs a listener might enjoy - **(C)** Awarding a scholarship based on a student's personal essay Where could mistakes cause harm, and who should be responsible? ::: {.notes} For each problem, choose a starting point and explain why. You can combine approaches. Take about a minute with your neighbour, and also consider where mistakes could cause harm. [Allow about one minute, then take responses.] For the email suffix, the logic is precise: check whether the address ends with the specified text. For song recommendations, we might learn patterns from listeners' preferences because those patterns are difficult to write down as complete rules. For a scholarship essay, we need accountable human judgment about criteria and context. A model might assist, but a predicted score doesn't settle who deserves the award. The consequences matter too: a poor song suggestion and an unfair scholarship decision have very different stakes. Making a prediction doesn't automatically justify handing the decision to a model. ::: ## (Optional) AI in the news {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **[Mathematical discovery](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cy7zygy3rl2o):** OpenAI reports an AI-generated solution to a major problem about fluid motion. **[Emotional support](https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ai-teenagers-mental-health-study-9.7327227):** About one in five students in an Ontario study reported seeking emotional support from AI. The association with emotional problems does not establish causation. ::: :::{.column width="50%"} ![](img/ai-math-problem.png) ![](img/ai-therapist.png) ::: :::: **What would you want to know before trusting an AI system in either setting?** ::: {.notes} [Optional discussion; use only if time remains after the reflection.] These reports give us two settings in which people may be tempted to trust an AI output: mathematical discovery and emotional support. What evidence would you want before trusting a system in either setting? [Take a few responses.] For a mathematical result, I'd want to know whether the argument has been independently checked and whether it answers the original question. A reported solution still needs verification. For emotional support, I'd ask how benefits and harms were evaluated, who was included, and how privacy and difficult situations are handled. An association between AI use and emotional problems doesn't establish that one caused the other. The connection to today's lecture is evaluation: an impressive output, or success on familiar examples, doesn't settle performance in a new setting. Treat these reports as starting points for questions about evidence. ::: ## Rules, ML, or human judgment? {.smaller visibility="hidden"} | Starting point | When it is appropriate | |---|---| | **Explicit rules** | The logic is known, stable, and can be stated precisely. | | **Machine learning** | Useful patterns exist in representative data, hand-written rules are difficult, and we can evaluate errors. | | **Human judgment** | Context, empathy, values, or accountability are central to the decision. | Real systems can combine all three. Making a prediction does not automatically justify delegating the decision to a model. ::: {.notes} [Optional hidden reference slide.] This table summarizes our discussion. Explicit rules work well when the logic is known and can be stated precisely. Machine learning can help when representative data contain useful patterns, rules are difficult to write, and we can evaluate the errors. Human judgment matters when context, values, empathy, and accountability are central. Real systems can combine these approaches. Human oversight also needs careful design; adding a person doesn't automatically make a system reliable. ::: # Formulate a prediction problem ::: {.notes} We've used cats and foxes to introduce learning from examples. Now let's formulate a prediction problem using a small table of job attributes. We'll use the same dataset to build a baseline and a decision tree. ::: ## Which job might make you happy? {.slide-your-turn} You've graduated and have several job offers. **Which one would make you happiest?** ![](img/happy-vs-sad-employee.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" width="400px" fig-alt="Happy vs sad employees"}
Image created by GPT-6 Astra
- **What job attributes would you record?** - **What outcome would you predict, and how would you represent it?** ::: {.notes} Imagine you've graduated and you're comparing job offers. Which job might make you happiest? What attributes would you record before trying to answer that? [Take two or three suggestions.] You might record salary, support from colleagues, or other things you value. Now think about the outcome: would you record Happy or Unhappy, or a satisfaction score from zero to one hundred? Those choices produce different prediction tasks. Coding Happy as one doesn't turn it into a numerical quantity in the same sense as a satisfaction score. We'll use an invented dataset to explore the workflow. It won't tell us what causes happiness or make a job decision for us. ::: ## Toy job happiness dataset ::: {#8cd91166 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Supportive
colleagues		 Salary ($) Free
coffee		 Boss
vegan		 Happy?

1 150,000 1 1 Happy

``` ::: ::: Each row describes one person in a job. **1 = yes; 0 = no.** ::: {.notes} Here are our seven examples. Each row represents one person in a job. Let's read the first row together: no supportive colleagues, a salary of seventy thousand, no free coffee, and a vegan boss. This person reported being Unhappy. For the yes-or-no attributes, one means yes and zero means no. Salary is a numerical amount. The final column contains the known happiness label. The boss's diet is an arbitrary candidate feature in this toy dataset. Recording something doesn't make it useful, and it doesn't show that it causes the outcome. Which columns should we give the model, and which column should we ask it to predict? ::: ## Your turn: identify $X$ and $y$ {.slide-your-turn} ::: {#741e3d96 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Supportive
colleagues		 Salary ($) Free
coffee		 Boss

``` ::: ::: First three examples: **which columns are inputs, and which is the target?** ::: {.fragment} **Features $X$:** the four job attributes \ **Target $y$:** `Happy?`\ **Example:** one row \ $n = 7$ examples and $d = 4$ features ::: ::: {.notes} Look at these first three examples and identify three things: the inputs X, the target y, and what counts as one example. [Pause before revealing the answer.] The four job attributes are the features. The happy? column is the target. One row is one example: a person in a job. We're displaying three rows, but the complete dataset has seven examples, so n is seven. There are four features, so d is four. The target isn't included in that feature count. The inputs must be available when we make a prediction. We can't include the unknown happiness answer as one of the clues. ::: ## Training vs. Prediction - Training: learn the mapping - Known features $X$ + known targets $y$ $\to$ fitted model $f$ - Prediction: use the mapping - New features $X_{\text{new}}$ $\to$ fitted model $f$ $\to$ predictions $\hat{y}_{\text{new}}$ **We need known targets to train the model, not to make predictions.** ::: {.notes} Let's separate two stages. During training, we have the job attributes and the known happiness labels. We use them to fit a model that relates inputs to targets. During prediction, the model is already fitted. We provide the attributes of a new job example, and it returns a proposed happiness label. Prediction doesn't itself retrain the model. We write y for an actual target and y-hat for a prediction. The hat reminds us that this is an estimate, and it can be wrong. Known targets are needed to train this supervised model and to evaluate its predictions. They aren't needed to produce predictions. ::: ## Same job features, different targets {.smaller} ::: {#a67998a8 .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Supportive

coffee		 Boss

``` ::: ::: - **Happy or unhappy** $\to$ predict a discrete label $\to$ **classification** - **Happiness score from 0 to 100** $\to$ predict a numerical quantity $\to$ **regression** Other regression examples: predicting temperature, house price, or travel time. ::: {.notes} We can keep the job features the same and change the target. If we ask Happy or Unhappy, we're predicting a category. That's classification. If we ask for a happiness score from zero to one hundred, we're predicting a numerical quantity. That's regression. These scores are invented for illustration. The two outcome columns represent alternative questions. If we're predicting an unknown satisfaction score, we shouldn't quietly give the model the person's happiness label as an input. The distinction depends on what the answer means. A category stored as zero or one is still a category. Other regression targets include temperature, house price, and travel time. ::: ## iClicker 1.1: Classification or regression? {.slide-your-turn} **Select all regression problems.** - **A.** Predict whether a flight will be delayed. - **B.** Predict a flight's delay in minutes - **C.** Predict a student's percentage grade in DSCI 571. - **D.** Predict whether you'll get a seat on the bus. - **E.** Predict whether you'll hit snooze tomorrow morning. ::: {.notes} Select all the regression problems. Focus on the kind of answer each question asks for. [Allow 30–60 seconds for responses.] The answers are B and C. Delay in minutes and percentage grade are numerical quantities. A, D, and E ask for yes-or-no categories, so they're classification. Notice that A and B describe the same flight context, but the targets differ. Whether a flight is delayed is a category; how many minutes it's delayed is a quantity. For C, a percentage grade is a regression target. If we changed the question to predicting a letter-grade category, we'd have a classification problem. ::: # Train, predict, and evaluate models using `scikit-learn` ::: {.notes} Now we'll implement the problem in scikit-learn. We'll begin with a deliberately simple model, so we have a reference point for judging whether a decision tree improves the predictions. ::: ## Separate the inputs from the target ::: {#ee9c1ae6 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = toy_happiness_df.drop(columns=['happy?']) y = toy_happiness_df['happy?'] ``` ::: | Object | Contains | Shape | |---|---|---| | `X` | Four feature values for each person | `(7, 4)` | | `y` | One known happiness label per person | `(7,)` | **Keep the answer out of the inputs.** ::: {.notes} The first line builds X by dropping the happy? column from the table. The second line selects that column as y. These lines organize the data; they don't train anything yet. X has shape seven by four: seven examples, each with four feature values. y has shape seven: one label for each example. Each label must stay aligned with its corresponding row in X. Why do we remove happy? from X? Because that's the answer we're trying to predict. Including it would give the model information we wouldn't have for a new person. Before using the features, let's see how well we can do by ignoring them. ::: ## Your turn: predict without the features {.slide-your-turn} ![](img/happy_unhappy_faces.png){.nostretch width="320px" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Seven training labels: four Happy and three Unhappy"} If you must predict **the same label for everyone**, which label should you choose? How many predictions will be correct? ::: {.notes} Suppose you're required to predict the same label for every person. You can't use salary, colleagues, or any other feature. Which label should you choose, and how many predictions would be correct? [Allow 30–45 seconds.] There are four Happy labels and three Unhappy labels, so choose Happy. That gives four correct predictions out of seven. Choosing Unhappy would give three. This is a most-frequent baseline. It uses the training labels to choose a constant answer, but it ignores the job attributes. ::: ## A baseline gets four out of seven right ::: {#f2f34f2d .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Actual Baseline prediction Correct?
Unhappy Happy No
Unhappy Happy No
Happy Happy Yes
Happy Happy Yes
Happy Happy Yes
Happy Happy Yes
Unhappy Happy No
``` ::: ::: **Always predict Happy:** accuracy $= 4/7 \approx 57\%$\ **Classification error:** $3/7 \approx 43\% = 1 - \text{accuracy}$ ::: {.notes} Here's what always predicting Happy looks like row by row. A person whose actual label is Happy is classified correctly. A person whose actual label is Unhappy is classified incorrectly. Accuracy is the number of correct predictions divided by the total number of predictions. Here that's four divided by seven, or about 57 percent. Classification error is the fraction incorrect: three divided by seven, or about 43 percent. For this measure, error is one minus accuracy. This gives us a reference point on the training examples. Let's reproduce it with scikit-learn. ::: ## Fit a baseline with scikit-learn We’ll use [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/), a Python machine learning library. ::: {#0904d95b .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent') dummy.fit(X, y); ``` ::: **`fit(X, y)`** learns from the training data. Here, it finds the most frequent target. **This baseline ignores the feature values.** ::: {.notes} Scikit-learn is the Python machine learning library we'll use. First we import DummyClassifier, the estimator class. Then we create an estimator and choose the most_frequent strategy. Finally, we call fit with X and y. Creating dummy gives us a model object with a specified strategy. Calling fit uses the training data to determine which label is most frequent. In this dataset, that label is Happy. This strategy accepts X to keep the interface consistent with other estimators, but it ignores the feature values. Its learned answer comes from the labels. Salary is another candidate. ::: ## How does a tree learn its questions? - Learn **which feature-based questions to ask, and in what order**. - At each node, compare candidate questions and choose a split that makes the groups' labels less mixed. - Repeat within each group, until a stopping condition is reached. - Each leaf predicts its most frequent training class. ::: {.notes} A tree automates the comparison we just made. At a node, it considers questions about the features and chooses a split that makes the resulting groups' labels less mixed. Then it repeats that process within each group. It stops when a stopping condition is met, such as a depth limit or a group whose labels are already all the same. At a leaf, it predicts the most frequent training class among the examples that reached that leaf. Measures such as Gini impurity or entropy quantify how mixed the labels are. We won't need their formulas today. Numerical features work too: a question can be salary less than or equal to a threshold. These choices are made locally, so they don't guarantee the best possible whole tree. Let's see what this algorithm learns. ::: ## Fit a decision tree ::: {#d24730d6 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=1) model.fit(X, y); ``` ::: **Same `fit` interface. A different learning algorithm.** `max_depth=2` allows at most two questions along a prediction path. ::: {.notes} The code has the same pattern as the baseline: import the estimator, create it, and call fit with X and y. This time the estimator is DecisionTreeClassifier. We've set max_depth to two. That means the tree can ask at most two questions along any path from the root to a leaf. It doesn't mean there are only two questions in the whole tree, and some paths may be shorter. We've also set random_state so the example is reproducible. Calling fit now selects the questions and leaf predictions using our training data. Let's inspect the fitted tree rather than treating it as a black box. ::: ## Read the learned tree {.smaller} ::: {#0d061075 .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-01-intro-terminology-decision-trees_files/figure-revealjs/cell-14-output-1.png){width=1192 height=607} ::: ::: **Root:** first question, **Branch:** answer to a question, **Leaf:** prediction ::: {.notes} Start at the top, called the root. The first question is: is salary less than or equal to seventy-five thousand? In this plot, True goes left and False goes right. If salary is at most seventy-five thousand, we reach a leaf that predicts Unhappy. If salary is higher, we ask whether supportive_colleagues is less than or equal to point five. Since this feature is zero or one, that means: are supportive colleagues absent? Zero goes left to Unhappy; one goes right to Happy. A branch represents an answer, and a leaf gives the prediction. The samples count tells us how many training examples reached a node. The value counts are in Happy, Unhappy order. The leaf chooses the majority class. Salary was selected first because the algorithm compared more candidates than our earlier two-question exercise. ::: ## Prediction {.model-plot .boundary-plot} What would be the prediction for the example below using this tree ? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {#3ab83362 .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-01-intro-terminology-decision-trees_files/figure-revealjs/cell-16-output-1.png){width=1192 height=607} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} - supportive_colleagues = 0 - salary = 100,000 - coffee_machine = 0 - vegan_boss = 1 ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Try this example yourselves before we trace it together. Coffee and the boss's diet don't appear in this tree's questions, so they don't affect this path.
